task_title: Communications, Light Signals, and Runway Lighting Systems
area: Area VI. Airport and Seaplane Base Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain frequencies, standard phraseology, the transponder, radar assistance, light gun signals, lost communication procedures and Runway Status Lights at commercial-pilot depth, and teach a nervous learner to use the radio with confidence, handle a radio failure and decide when to declare an emergency.
why: Many learners find the radio harder than the flying, and fear blocks learning [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. The AIM calls radio communication a critical link that can break with surprising speed and disastrous results [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]]. As the instructor you decide whether a learner hides behind your voice or becomes a calm, clear communicator who asks ATC for help early.

prereading.what: Radio technique, contact procedures, call signs, student pilot identification, radio failure at a tower, light gun signals and readbacks.

prereading.label: AIM 6-1-1 to 6-4-3

prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.3, 91.123, 91.125, 91.129, 91.185
prereading.what: Emergency authority, compliance with ATC, light signals, Class D communications failure and IFR radio failure.

prereading.label: PHAK 14-22 to 14-25

prereading.label: AFH 8-6, 18-1, 18-13, 18-14

prereading.label: AIH 1-20 to 10-9 (selected pages)
prereading.what: Declaring emergencies, ATC as a resource, fear and perception, schemas, short-term memory, scenarios, solo readiness and teaching without blocking the radio.

warmup: Think first: your new learner flies the airplane well, but when you hand her the radio she keys the mike, says "um, Cessna, um," and lets go. Afterward she tells you she is afraid of sounding stupid in front of everyone on the frequency. What is going on in her head, what would you change in the next lesson, and how would you know it worked?

key_terms.def: The first call to a facility or to a new controller: facility name, full call sign, position if on the airport surface, then the request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]].
Saying "student pilot" on the initial call so ATC can give extra help and consideration [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4]].
"Repeat my message back to me." Airborne pilots read back altitudes, vectors and runway assignments [[34:404|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].
I can't comply with that specific instruction, request or clearance [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]].
Please repeat the last transmission, or the part named [[34:413|AIM P/C Glossary]].
With a frequency change: listen on that frequency and stand by; normally do not call [[34:381|AIM P/C Glossary]].
Establish communication with the named facility, on the frequency given [[34:329|AIM P/C Glossary]].

Concern about safety that needs timely but not immediate help [[34:437|AIM P/C Glossary]]. You are in it the moment you doubt your position, fuel, weather or anything else affecting safety [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].
Tower's hand-held light with a narrow white, green or red beam, used to approve or disapprove a pilot's expected actions when radio is not available [[34:373|AIM P/C Glossary]].
The transponder code for loss of two-way radio communication [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].
Red in-pavement lights from the hold line to the runway that show high-speed traffic on the runway or an aircraft on final [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].
Two rows of red in-pavement lights beside the runway centerline that show it is unsafe to take off because the runway is or is about to be occupied [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6]].

chunks.title: Why learners fear the radio, and what fear does to learning

body.p: Speaking in public is high on many people's list of fears. Fear triggers fight or flight: one person avoids the job, another learns ways to cope with it [[25:34|AIH 2-1]]. Application: a learner keying the mike on a busy frequency is speaking in public, so expect the same reactions.

Fear narrows perception. A frightened learner focuses on the thing that scares her. A situation that feels overwhelming is a threat; one she feels able to handle is a challenge [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]. Emotions also block listening: an instrument learner who expects big routing changes gets anxious and can hardly take in the new route [[25:101|AIH 4-8]].

head: What you see
What the AIH says
What you do
rows: The learner hears every "the" and "and" but misses the altitude
Beginners lack a schema. An experienced pilot knows a clearance holds a few key items and is primed to catch them [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]
Teach the shape of each call before the words: what ATC will give, and in what order
The learner reads back a frequency, then dials the wrong one
Short-term memory holds about 30 seconds and about seven chunks; it takes 5 to 10 seconds to code, and an interruption loses it [[25:87|AIH 3-36]]
Write it down as it is spoken; never talk to the learner while ATC is talking
"I'll sound stupid"
A negative self-concept puts up barriers to perceiving and performing [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]
Plan early successes: ATIS first, then ground, then tower
The learner fumbles two radios
Errors with two radios drop quickly once learners understand each radio's purpose [[25:85|AIH 3-34]]
Give each radio a job: COM1 for ATC, COM2 for ATIS

callout.text: Tell the learner on day one: a student pilot who says "student pilot" on the initial call gets extra help and consideration from ATC. The AIM recommends it on each initial contact with clearance delivery, ground, tower, approach, departure and FSS [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4]].

check.q: Your learner is calm on the ground but goes silent when approach gives a long instruction in flight. Which AIH idea explains it?
check.a: Fear and anxiety narrow perception and block listening [[25:59|AIH 3-8]] [[25:101|AIH 4-8]]. Lower the threat: teach the shape of the call on the ground and build up in small steps.

chunks.title: K1 and S1: Getting the frequencies and setting them right

body.p: The full frequency tables are in the Commercial lesson CA.III.A; here is what to teach. Airport data comes from aeronautical charts, the Chart Supplement (the most complete source, revised every 56 days), NOTAMs and ATIS [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]]. The CTAF is in the Chart Supplement and on instrument approach and departure charts, or ask any FSS [[33:207|AIM 4-1-9]]. Most ground control frequencies are 121.6 to 121.9 MHz [[33:257|AIM 4-3-14]]. Unsure en route? 122.2 MHz reaches most FSSs [[33:235|AIM 4-2-14]]. 121.5 MHz is the emergency frequency, guarded by most civil towers and radar facilities [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]].
In flight, ATC hands off with "contact" (establish communication) or "monitor" (listen and stand by, normally without calling) [[34:329|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:381|AIM P/C Glossary]].

bullets: Civil VHF radios use 118.000 to 136.975 MHz. You need 25 kHz spacing to use the whole system; if ATC assigns a frequency you can't select, ask for another [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].
Many radios store one or more frequencies while one stays active for transmitting and receiving [[23:53|IFH 2-2]]. Application: teach "next frequency in standby" as a habit.
VHF is line of sight, so higher altitude means longer range [[1:356|PHAK 14-22]].
Tune and verify frequencies before entering the airport traffic area [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].
The audio panel sets receiver volume and selects the transmitter, with speaker and headphone positions [[23:53|IFH 2-2]].
The COM1/COM2 selector changes both transmit and receive. Use it to hear ATIS on one radio while you stay with ATC on the other [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
A headset with a boom mike close to the lips beats a hand mike and cabin speaker [[23:53|IFH 2-2]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].
After any change, pause and listen so you don't step on someone [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

callout.text: Application: before every flight, have the learner write a frequency card in the order of use and say each frequency out loud as it goes into standby. It turns frequency handling into a habit and shows you at once who is lost.

check.q: Approach says, "Monitor tower one one eight point three." Your learner switches and calls tower right away. What do you teach?
check.a: Monitor means listen and stand by for instructions; under normal circumstances don't call [[34:381|AIM P/C Glossary]]. "Contact" would mean establish communication [[34:329|AIM P/C Glossary]].

chunks.title: K2 and S2: Teaching standard phraseology one block at a time

body.p: The most important thought in pilot and controller talk is understanding. Acknowledge each call with your call sign, keep it brief, but use whatever words you need [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]]. Good phraseology is the mark of a professional, and the Pilot/Controller Glossary is the same one controllers use [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].
New learning is built on a solid base, and correct habits are much easier to build from the start than to fix later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Teach the radio in blocks:

head: Block
What the learner masters
Source
rows: 1. Listen
ATIS, heard as many times as needed when the cockpit is quiet; report the code letter on initial contact
2. Technique
Listen before you transmit, think before you key, mike close, slight pause after pressing, normal tone, wait a few seconds before calling again
3. Initial contact
Facility, full call sign, position if on the surface, request. Type or maker, then registration without the N. Phonetic alphabet for the call sign
4. Readbacks
Altitudes, vectors and runway assignments, in the order given, with the call sign
5. Exact words
Wilco (will comply), Unable, Say again, Stand by (neither approval nor denial)
[[34:445|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:413|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[34:420|AIM P/C Glossary]]
6. Busy airspace
VFR traffic advisories and arrivals with approach control: position, altitude, call sign, type, code, destination, request

callout.text: Never abbreviate a call sign on initial contact or when similar call signs are on frequency; pilots have flown clearances meant for someone else. If in doubt, say "verify clearance for" and your complete call sign [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].
Application: write a script for each block, then take it away one word at a time. The schema stays when the paper goes [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

check.q: On a busy frequency, ATC has already called your learner "Cessna Two Kilo Lima." May she use that short form too?
check.a: Yes. Once ATC starts using the prefix and last three characters after contact, the pilot may use the abbreviated call sign too, but not on an initial call [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]].

chunks.title: S3: Acknowledge and comply, or say unable

body.p: Acknowledge every callup and clearance unless told otherwise, with your call sign and Wilco, Roger, Affirmative, Negative or another fitting reply. If the situation demands it, act or tell the facility about any problem right away [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

head: What ATC says
What the learner does
rows: "Contact departure one two four point three five"
Acknowledge, switch as soon as possible, listen, then call. Switching without acknowledging leaves the controller wondering if you had a radio failure [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]] [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]
"Change to my frequency one two five point six"
Same controller, new frequency, so a short callup is fine: "one two five point six, Two Kilo Lima" [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]
"Turn left heading two four zero, climb and maintain three thousand five hundred"
Read back in the same order with the call sign [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]
"Stand by"
Wait. It is not an approval or denial; call again if the delay gets long [[34:420|AIM P/C Glossary]]
A clearance the learner did not catch
"Say again" or ask for clarification right away [[34:413|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]
A vector that would put a VFR learner into cloud
"Unable" with the reason. Vectors never authorize breaking a rule, and you should keep ATC told about the weather [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]] [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]

callout.text: If you are uncertain of a clearance, ask for clarification immediately. Once you accept one, don't deviate unless it is amended, an emergency exists, or you follow a TCAS RA. Except in an emergency, don't operate contrary to an ATC instruction where ATC is exercised [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]. Accepting or refusing a clearance is the pilot's job [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

body.p: Application: on the CFI practical test the evaluator may play ATC or tell you what to do. Treat those instructions exactly like real ones: acknowledge, read back the numbers, comply, or say unable.

check.q: Why should a learner acknowledge a frequency change before switching instead of just switching?
check.a: Without the acknowledgment the controller can't tell if the instruction was received or the radio failed, which adds to the controller's workload [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

chunks.title: Teaching with recorded and live ATC

body.p: The FAA sources do not describe teaching with ATC recordings or online live streams. What follows mixes source guidance with technique marked as application.

bullets: Start with what the AIM offers free: listen first, because you can often get what you need from ATIS or the frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]], and ATIS can be heard as many times as you like [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]].

Application: on the ground, play recordings of your local tower and approach. Pause before each pilot reply and have the learner say it, then compare. This builds the schema of what each call holds [[25:62|AIH 3-11]].

Use local scenarios. A good scenario has clear objectives, fits the learner and uses the local environment [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Application: rehearse the exact calls for your own airport and the approach facility you really use.

In the airplane, do most of the teaching before you call tower or announce on the CTAF. Teaching during the takeoff can cause missed transmissions and overload the learner [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]. On approach, use only short prompts [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].
Teach and model a sterile flight deck in critical phases of flight [[25:179|AIH 9-9]].
Hand over the radio in steps: ATIS, then ground, then tower, then approach. Application of the building-block idea [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

callout.text: Never coach over ATC. Pilots must stay alert to the ATC frequency for traffic conflicts, especially on an active runway or on final [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]]. A CFI talking in the headset is a distraction, not help.
Supervised solo: if possible carry a portable radio so you can end the solo if something develops, keep calls to the minimum, and never talk to the learner on short final [[25:182|AIH 9-12]].

check.q: You want to explain crosswind technique while the learner lines up on the runway and tower is talking. What does the AIH suggest?
check.a: Do that teaching before contacting tower. During the takeoff the learner may not process it, and you risk missed transmissions from tower [[25:192|AIH 10-8]].

chunks.title: K4 and K7: Transponder and radar assistance, taught as tools to ask for

body.p: Navigation Systems and Radar Services (AI.II.H) covers transponder modes, ADS-B and radar services in depth. For this Task, teach the habits:

head: When
What the learner does
rows: On any part of the movement area
Transponder in the altitude-reporting mode and ADS-B Out on; STBY or OFF at the parking spot [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20]]
In controlled airspace
Assigned code with altitude reporting; ADS-B Out transmitting at all times unless ATC says otherwise [[33:221|AIM 4-1-20]]
VFR, no code assigned
First call to an ATC facility
Report exact altitude to the nearest 100 feet [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]
"Ident"
Press IDENT only when asked [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]], and say you did [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]
Changing codes
Lost two-way radio / emergency not in contact
Before using it
The transponder must have been tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months [[60:525|14 CFR 91.413]]

body.p: Radar assistance: radar facilities give vectors to VFR aircraft that can talk to them, are in radar coverage and can be identified. The vectors are advisory, never permission to break a rule, and flying safely stays the pilot's job. Keep the controller told about the weather you are in and ahead [[33:217|AIM 4-1-17]]. All radar facilities give VFR aircraft safety alerts, traffic advisories, limited vectoring when workload permits, and sequencing where set up [[33:218|AIM 4-1-18]].

The teaching point: when learners use ATC in training, they gain the confidence to ask controllers to clarify instructions and to use ATC for help in unusual situations [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]. Before solo, learners should be taught to ask the ATC system for help when needed [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

callout.text: VFR in difficulty: a pilot without an instrument rating who can't stay VFR should tell the controller, say there is no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition. An instrument-rated, current pilot in an equipped airplane should request an IFR clearance [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

check.q: Approach tells your learner, "Radar service terminated, squawk VFR, frequency change approved." What does she do?
check.a: She no longer gets radar services [[34:403|AIM P/C Glossary]], sets 1200 [[33:222|AIM 4-1-20]] and may leave the frequency.

chunks.title: K3: ATC light signals, and how to make them stick

body.p: Towers use the light gun for aircraft without radio, and for radio-equipped aircraft when radio contact can't be made [[33:256|AIM 4-3-13]] [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]]. The meanings are set in regulation [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. The full table is in CA.III.A and PA.III.A; here is how to teach it.

bullets: Limits: the pilot may not be looking at the tower, and a light can only approve or disapprove what the pilot seems about to do. No extra information can be sent except the "general warning signal," which tells the pilot to be on the alert [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]]. The signal table also lists alternating red and green, meaning exercise extreme caution [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].
Acknowledge on the ground: ailerons or rudder by day, blink landing or navigation lights at night [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]].
Acknowledge in flight: rock the wings by day, blink landing or navigation lights at night [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].
At night on the ground, to get the tower's attention, turn on a landing light and taxi clear of the active runway where the tower can see it [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]].

head: Color
Teach it as
On the ground / in flight [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]
rows: Steady green
The final "yes"
Cleared for takeoff / cleared to land
Flashing green
"Yes" to the step before
Cleared to taxi / return for landing, steady green to follow
Steady red
"No, wait"
Stop / give way and keep circling
Flashing red
"Get away from the runway"
Taxi clear of the runway in use / airport unsafe, do not land
Flashing white
"Go back"
Return to starting point on airport / not applicable

callout.text: Application: first ask "Am I on the ground or in the air?" Then green means yes (steady is the last step, flashing the step before), red means no, white means go back.

check.q: Tower aims a steady red at your learner on downwind while her head is down resetting the radio. What limit of light signals does this show, and what do you teach?
check.a: Pilots may not be looking at the tower when a signal is sent [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]]. With a radio problem, teach her to keep watching the tower for light signals once she joins the pattern [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

chunks.title: K6: Equipment issues that can cut communication

body.p: CA.III.A lists the symptoms. As an instructor, teach a troubleshooting flow so the learner checks the simple things before declaring the radio dead.

head: Check
Why
Source
rows: Volume, frequency, stuck mike
Be alert to sounds or the lack of them; a stuck mike can block a frequency for a long time
Range
Remote sites may not receive on every frequency, especially at VORs; higher altitude increases VHF range
Audio panel
Wrong transmitter or receiver selected; COM1/COM2 changes both
Frequency spacing
Some radios can't select an assigned frequency; ask for another
Another transmitter, a short call
If no answer, recheck the radios or use another transmitter and keep the next call short; or call "any radio" for a call on a frequency
Electrical system
Most electrical failures are in the alternator or generator, and the battery may give very little time

body.p: A 25 amp-hour battery could supply 5 amps for 5 hours, but at 10 amps it might last only 2 hours, and a 40-amp load could empty it in about 10 to 15 minutes. An old battery or a late-detected failure gives less. Shed nonessential loads at once and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Figure 18-9 shows a keyed transceiver drawing 5 to 7 amps and two landing lights 17.80 amps [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

bullets: If a complete loss of electrical power is coming: shed all but the most necessary equipment, notify ATC immediately and request vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and expect a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension where those are electric [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].
Unless a fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, turning off the master kills the radios for a distress call and makes ATC lose the transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

check.q: Your learner's low-voltage light comes on and the radios start to fade. She wants to stay quiet on the radio to save the battery. What does the AFH say?
check.a: Any loss of electrical power is critical: shed nonessential loads, notify ATC immediately and request vectors to the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

chunks.title: K5: Lost communication procedures, and how to teach them

body.p: Whether a radio failure is an emergency is the pilot's call [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]]. In an in-flight emergency requiring immediate action, 14 CFR 91.3(b) lets the PIC deviate from any rule of part 91 to the extent needed to meet it [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. Squawk 7600, and remember you may be outside radar coverage [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

head: Arriving at a tower with
Do this [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]
rows: Receiver dead

Stay outside or above the Class D surface area until you know the direction and flow of traffic. Tell the tower your type, position, altitude and intention to land, and ask to be controlled with light signals. At 3 to 5 miles report your position and join the pattern, watch for lights, and report downwind and base if you fly a full pattern
Transmitter dead

Stay outside or above until you know the flow, join the pattern, monitor the tower frequency shown on the sectional, and watch for lights. Acknowledge by rocking the wings by day or blinking landing or navigation lights at night
Both dead
Stay outside or above until you know the flow, join the pattern and keep visual contact with the tower for light signals

callout.text: In Class D you must keep two-way radio communication. If the radio fails in flight under VFR, you may land if the weather is at or above basic VFR minimums, you keep visual contact with the tower, and you receive a clearance to land. Under IFR, follow 14 CFR 91.185 [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129]].

bullets: Radio dead before you leave the parking area: get it fixed, or phone the tower and ask to depart without two-way radio [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].
Busy airports don't accept no-radio (NORDO) arrivals [[1:357|PHAK 14-23]]. A non-towered airport with less traffic may be the wiser choice; watch extra carefully there [[1:358|PHAK 14-24]].
Remind every learner that aircraft without radios may be in any pattern [[24:170|AFH 8-6]].

IFR learners: in VFR conditions, continue VFR and land as soon as practicable [[60:482|14 CFR 91.185]]; otherwise fly the route, altitude and clearance-limit rules of 91.185 (see CA.III.A). To reestablish contact, try the last assigned frequency, an FSS, New York or San Francisco Radio and 121.5, all at once if you can [[34:54|AIM 6-4-3]] [[34:55|AIM 6-4-3]].

body.p: How to teach it: scenario-based training lets the learner visualize a normal flight, then you add the unexpected, such as a radio outage, and ask questions to check the thinking [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. The AIH low-fuel example grows in steps: recall in the classroom, then perform at the home airport, then on a cross-country with other duties [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Application: run the radio-failure scenario the same way.

check.q: Your learner's receiver has failed but her transmitter works. Before entering the Class D surface area, what does she tell the tower?
check.a: After staying outside or above until she knows the traffic flow: her type, position, altitude, intention to land, and a request to be controlled with light signals [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

body.p: Runway Status Lights (RWSL) are fully automatic. Surveillance data turns on red in-pavement lights when a runway is unsafe to enter, cross, take off from or land on. RWSL is an independent safety layer that never gives or replaces a clearance, and controllers may not even see the lights change [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]]. Other runway and approach lighting is taught in AI.II.M; runway incursion habits in AI.II.C.

bullets: REL: in-pavement lights along the taxiway centerline from the hold line to the runway edge, plus one at the runway centerline. Red means high-speed traffic on the runway or an aircraft on final within the activation area [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].

For a departing aircraft, RELs ahead light at about 30 knots and go out 3 to 4 seconds before it reaches each intersection. For an arrival, they light when it is about 1 mile from the threshold [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].

Red REL: stop at the hold line or stay stopped and contact ATC if the clearance conflicts. If staying clear is unsafe, for example you are already on the runway, use your best judgment and call ATC as soon as possible [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].

THL: two rows beside the centerline lights, 1,500 feet long, starting 375 feet from the departure threshold. They need two players: an aircraft in position or rolling, and another aircraft or vehicle on or about to enter the runway [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6]].
Lights going out is not a takeoff clearance [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6]]. Red THLs: stop if you safely can, or stay stopped, and contact ATC [[33:128|AIM 2-1-6]] [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6]].

Pilot actions: transponder and ADS-B on from leaving the parking area until shutdown there; always tell the tower when you stop for RWSL; never cross red lights; don't move when lights go out without a clearance [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6]].
Controllers can set five brightness levels, and when the system or part of it is disabled a NOTAM is issued and the ATIS updated [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6]].

callout.text: Application: most training airports have no RWSL, so learners meet it for the first time on a cross-country. Brief it before any trip to an airport that has it, and drill the rule in one line: red means stop and talk, dark means nothing without a clearance.

check.q: Who can change RWSL brightness, and how will your learner know if the system is turned off?
check.a: Controllers can set the lights to one of five brightness levels. If the system or a part is disabled, a NOTAM is issued and the ATIS is updated [[33:129|AIM 2-1-6]].

chunks.title: R1: Communication risks for the learner and the instructor

body.p: Voice radio is a hazard detector: controllers and flight service give real-time information on weather, traffic, airspace and other hazards [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. When the link fails or is used badly, risk goes up.

head: Risk
What it looks like
Mitigation
rows: Wrong aircraft takes a clearance
Similar call signs and a short readback
Full call signs; "verify clearance for" when in doubt [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
Silent frequency change
Learner switches without acknowledging
Acknowledge first [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]]
Instructor blocks the radio
CFI coaching on takeoff or final; missed calls
Teach before calling tower; short prompts only [[25:192|AIH 10-8]] [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Learner leans on the instructor's voice
CFI makes every call
Use ATC in training so the learner builds confidence [[25:29|AIH 1-25]]
Blocked frequency
Long silence, then a stuck-mike report
Check your own mike; ATC may move everyone to another frequency [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]
Talking instead of flying
Head down on the radio during an emergency
There may be no time to contact ATC in an emergency; prioritize the tasks [[30:56|RMH 8-3]]

body.p: English proficiency is part of communication risk. During training, a flight review or any regulatory check, the person conducting it should evaluate whether the pilot meets the FAA Aviation English Language Standard [[10:4|AC 60-28B 6]]. An "English Proficient" endorsement means at least ICAO Level 4 [[10:5|AC 60-28B 6.4]].

callout.text: Expectation bias in taxi clearances is taught in AI.II.C. Here, watch for its radio cousin: the learner who reads back what she expected, not what was said. Make her write it first.

check.q: On a flight review, the pilot flies well but you can barely understand her radio calls in English. What does AC 60-28B ask of you?
check.a: The person conducting a flight review should evaluate whether the pilot demonstrates the FAA Aviation English Language Standard [[10:4|AC 60-28B 6]].

chunks.title: R2: Deciding if and when to declare an emergency

body.p: Teach learners that declaring an emergency when one occurs is the right reaction; ATC then gives priority handling, and 14 CFR 91.3 lets the PIC deviate from any rule as needed. A learner who hesitates, or decides not to decide, has made a wrong decision [[25:24|AIH 1-20]].

Pilots declare distress readily for fire, mechanical failure or structural damage, but many are reluctant to report urgency. You are in at least an urgency condition the moment you doubt your position, fuel endurance, weather or anything else affecting safety; that is the time to ask for help. Delay has cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

head: The learner says
What the sources say
rows: "I'll get in trouble or buried in paperwork."

A written report of a 91.3(b) deviation is needed only if the FAA asks [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]. If ATC gave priority, a report within 48 hours to the facility manager only if ATC asks [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]
"It isn't bad enough yet."
Urgency starts at doubt [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Reluctance to accept the emergency leads to indecision and errors [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]
"I'll just say minimum fuel."
Minimum fuel is not an emergency and gets no priority. If you need priority to land safely, declare an emergency for low fuel and give fuel remaining in minutes [[34:10|AIM 5-5-15]]
"I don't know the words."
Plain language works: the difficulty, your intentions and the help you want. MAYDAY or PAN-PAN, preferably three times, has advantages [[34:45|AIM 6-3-1]]
"Is a dead radio an emergency?"
The pilot decides [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]]

bullets: After declaring: follow ATC's advice, ask when you don't understand, and don't change frequency unless you absolutely must [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
In contact with ATC, keep the assigned code unless told otherwise; if you can't reach ATC at once, squawk 7700 with Mode C [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

callout.text: Application: rehearse the distress and urgency calls on the ground and on the intercom until the words come without thought. The sources say nothing about practice calls on a live frequency, so keep practice off the air.

check.q: Your learner is unsure of her position with 45 minutes of fuel and says she will call ATC "if it turns into an emergency." What do you teach?
check.a: She is already in at least an urgency condition because she doubts her position; the AIM says ask for help now, not after it becomes distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

chunks.title: How to teach it: from the first ATIS to the solo cross-country

head: Stage
Learner does
Instructor does
rows: Ground, before flight 1
Builds a frequency list from the Chart Supplement and charts [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]]; listens to ATIS and recordings
Gives the shape of each call so the learner has a schema [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]
First flights
Copies ATIS, sets frequencies, listens
Makes the calls as a model; keeps critical phases sterile [[25:179|AIH 9-9]]
Ground control
Calls ground from a script
Coaches before keying, never over ATC [[25:192|AIH 10-8]]
Tower and pattern
Makes every pattern call
Uses only short prompts on approach [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]
Presolo
Uses proper radio procedure consistently and knows to ask ATC for help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]]; knows light signals and lost-comm steps
Briefs the solo; carries a portable radio if possible [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]
Cross-country
Flight following, radar help, a simulated radio failure scenario
Adds the unexpected and asks questions [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]

body.p: Insist on correct technique from the start; faulty habits are much harder to fix later [[25:91|AIH 3-40]]. Tell the learner after each lesson exactly how she is progressing; worry fades when nothing is withheld [[25:46|AIH 2-13]].

callout.text: When a radio error happens, ask the learner why it happened and what would prevent it. Some errors only need more practice; others show a habit to fix [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

check.q: Your learner flies the pattern well enough to solo but still lets you make most tower calls. Is she ready?
check.a: Not yet. Solo readiness includes consistent, proper radio procedure and communication skills, and knowing to ask ATC for help [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Transmitting without listening
Steps on another call right after a frequency change
Listen first; pause after every change [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]
Keying before thinking
"Um" and long gaps on the air
Know what to say first; jot long messages [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]
Clipped first word
ATC hears only the end of the call sign
Mike close to the lips; slight pause after pressing [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]]
Abbreviated or wrong call sign
ATC asks who called
Full call sign on initial contact; shorten only after ATC does [[33:229|AIM 4-2-4]]
"Roger" to a question
ATC has to ask again
Roger is not yes or no; use Affirmative, Negative or Unable [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Incomplete readback
Altitude or runway missing, items out of order
Altitudes, vectors and runways, in order, with call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]
Calling after "monitor"
An unneeded call on tower
Monitor means listen and stand by [[34:381|AIM P/C Glossary]]
Forgetting the ATIS code
Controller reads the weather to you
Say "information (code) received" on initial contact [[33:213|AIM 4-1-13]]
Pressing IDENT unasked, or passing 7700 on a code change
False alarms at ATC
IDENT only on request; change digits to avoid 7500, 76xx and 77xx [[33:223|AIM 4-1-20]]
Declaring radio failure too soon
Squawks 7600 after a quiet minute
Volume, frequency, stuck mike, audio panel first [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]] [[23:54|IFH 2-3]]
Mixing ground and air light meanings
Treats flashing green in flight as cleared to land
Ask "ground or air?" first [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]
Waiting too long to ask for help
"I didn't want to bother them"
Urgency starts at doubt; ask early [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]

check.q: Tower keeps hearing only "...Two Kilo Lima" from your learner. What is the likely error and the fix?
check.a: She talks the instant she presses the button, so the first word is lost. Keep the mike close and pause slightly after pressing [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

f1.caption: Figure 2-1. Typical navigation/communication installation (center stack only; the side callouts are trimmed for the labeling game). (IFH 2-2)
f1.alt: A radio stack: two com/nav radios each showing a USE and a STBY frequency with a swap button, an ADF, a GPS unit, and at the bottom a transponder showing code 1200 with an IDT button and a mode knob marked OFF, SBY, ON, ALT and TST.

f2.caption: Figure 2-2. Audio panel. (IFH 2-2)
f2.alt: An audio panel with marker beacon lights, intercom volume and pilot, crew, all switch, receiver buttons COM1, COM2, COM3, NAV1, NAV2, MKR, DME, ADF, AUX and MONI, and a microphone selector knob for C1, C2, C3, EMG and PA.

f3.caption: Figure 14-42. Light gun signals. (PHAK 14-25)
f3.alt: Table of tower light gun signals: steady green, flashing green, steady red, flashing red, flashing white and alternating red and green, with meanings for vehicles and personnel, aircraft on the ground and aircraft in flight.

f4.caption: FIG 2-1-10. Runway Entrance Lights. (AIM 2-1-6)
f4.alt: Photo at dusk from a taxiway at a runway hold line: a line of red in-pavement lights runs along the curved taxiway centerline from the hold line toward the runway.

f5.caption: AIM FIG 2-1-11. Takeoff Hold Lights. (AIM 2-1-6)
f5.alt: Photo down a runway at dusk: two rows of red lights on either side of the runway centerline, with an airliner crossing the runway far ahead.

f6.caption: Figure 18-9. Electrical load for light single. (AFH 18-14)
f6.alt: Table of electrical loads for a light single. Continuous loads such as pitot heat 3.30 amps, wingtip lights 3.00 amps, nav and com receivers 1 to 2 amps each. Intermittent loads such as starter 100 amps, landing lights 17.80, heater blower 14.00, flap motor 13.00 and keyed transceiver 5 to 7 amps.

scenario.title: The learner who would rather fly than talk
scenario.setup: Your learner has 25 hours, flies the airplane well and is close to solo at your non-towered home airport. She avoids the radio and gets quiet whenever approach calls. Next week you fly a dual cross-country with flight following to a Class D airport 60 miles away. The airplane has one alternator.

questions.q: What do you do on the ground before the flight?
questions.a: Have her build the frequency list from the Chart Supplement, charts and ATIS [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]] and script the calls so she has the shape of each one [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]. Start with what she can succeed at; fear narrows perception [[25:59|AIH 3-8]].

questions.q: She asks if it is all right to tell ATC she is a student. What do you say?
questions.a: Yes. The AIM recommends "student pilot" on each initial contact so ATC can give extra help [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4]].

questions.q: Approach gives a long instruction and she freezes. What do you coach, and when?
questions.a: After the transmission, a short prompt: "Say again" is fine [[34:413|AIM P/C Glossary]], and when unsure of a clearance she must ask at once [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]]. Don't talk over ATC [[25:193|AIH 10-9]].

questions.q: You want to practice a receiver failure near the Class D. How do you run it safely?
questions.a: Brief it on the ground and talk it through first [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]. Class D requires two-way radio communication [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129]], so as an application keep the real radio working and handle ATC yourself while she narrates the AIM steps [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

questions.q: On the way home the ammeter shows a discharge and the radios weaken. What should she do?
questions.a: Shed nonessential loads, notify ATC immediately and request vectors to the nearest suitable airport; the battery may last very little time [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

questions.q: In the debrief she says she didn't want to bother ATC with the problem. How do you answer?
questions.a: Using ATC in training builds confidence to ask for help [[25:29|AIH 1-25]], and the AIM says ask for help as soon as you are in doubt, not after things get worse [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

skills.do: Select and activate the right frequencies (ATIS, ground, tower or CTAF, approach, and 121.5 when needed), find them in the Chart Supplement, on charts or from ATC, and explain each choice and the audio panel setting as you would to a learner. The ACS gives no numeric tolerance for this CFI element (ACS AI.VI.A.S1).
skills.practice: Build a frequency card for each flight from the sources in PHAK 14-3 [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]] and set standby and the audio panel out loud [[23:54|IFH 2-3]].

skills.do: Transmit using standard phraseology and procedures as specified in the AIM and the Pilot/Controller Glossary: correct initial contact, full call sign, ATIS code, readbacks, and words like Wilco and Unable used correctly (ACS AI.VI.A.S2).
skills.practice: Use the AIM initial contact format on every flight [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]] and review the glossary from time to time as the AIM recommends [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].

skills.do: Acknowledge radio communications and comply with ATC instructions or as directed by the evaluator: read back altitudes, vectors and runways in order with your call sign, ask when unsure, and say unable when you can't comply (ACS AI.VI.A.S3).
skills.practice: Have a partner play ATC with clearances and vectors and read them back [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]]; practice asking for clarification [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors: the examiner plays a learner who clips words, says Roger to questions, misses a readback or misreads a light signal, and you name the error, its cause and the fix (ACS AI.VI.A.S4).
skills.practice: Rehearse each row of the common errors table with its AIM fix [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]] [[34:407|AIM P/C Glossary]], explaining it in one sentence.

quiz.q: Your learner assumes the tower is watching the Runway Status Lights and will warn her if they turn red. What does the AIM say?
options: Correct; the controller switches the lights by hand for each clearance
The lights only work when the tower is closed, so ATC never sees them
The tower turns them on only for jets, so a trainer will never see them
The system is automatic, and controllers may not even see the lights change
quiz.why: RWSL is fully automatic; ATC has limited control over it, and personnel do not directly use and may not be able to view the light activations during daily operations [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]]. RWSL never gives or replaces a clearance.

quiz.q: What should a student pilot add to an initial call to get extra help from ATC?
options: Code 7600
The word "training" in place of the call sign
The words "student pilot"
The instructor's name
quiz.why: Student pilots need only identify themselves as a student pilot on the initial call [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4]].

quiz.q: Your learner can't find the ground control frequency for a towered field and starts guessing. In what band does the AIM say most ground frequencies fall?
options: 118.0 to 118.9 MHz, the same block as the tower
121.6 to 121.9 MHz, the usual ground band
122.7 to 123.0 MHz, the CTAF and UNICOM block
121.5 MHz only, the guarded frequency
quiz.why: The majority of ground control frequencies are in the 121.6 to 121.9 MHz band [[33:257|AIM 4-3-14]]. The Chart Supplement lists the actual frequency [[1:337|PHAK 14-3]].

quiz.q: ATC answers your learner's request with "Stand by." What does that mean?
options: Wait; it is neither an approval nor a denial
The request is approved; go ahead when ready
The request is denied; ask again later if needed
Change to another frequency and call there
quiz.why: Stand by means pause a few seconds; it is not an approval or denial [[34:420|AIM P/C Glossary]].

quiz.q: Which parts of a clearance should an airborne pilot read back?
options: Only the call sign
Only the frequency changes
Everything, including charted altitudes on a DP
Altitudes, vectors and runway assignments
quiz.why: Read back altitude assignments, vectors and runway assignments; charted altitudes aren't read back unless the controller states them [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]] [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

quiz.q: Your learner keeps transmitting on the radio she set for ATIS. What does the AIH say makes two-radio errors drop quickly?
options: Practicing with only one radio until the checkride
Turning the second radio off whenever ATC is talking
Understanding each radio's specific purpose
Labeling the knobs with tape so they can't be mixed up
quiz.why: Errors with two radios, each with an active and standby frequency, drop quickly when learners understand each radio's specific purpose, such as ATIS on one and ATC on the other [[25:85|AIH 3-34]].

quiz.q: Besides approving or disapproving a pilot's expected action, what can the light gun tell a pilot?
options: The traffic to follow, by flashing toward it
Only a general warning to be on the alert
The runway in use, by pointing the beam at it
The wind and altimeter, by a coded flash
quiz.why: No explanatory information can be sent except the general warning signal [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]].

quiz.q: Your learner calls ground for the first time from the ramp. Under the AIM initial contact format, what does she include that an airborne call would leave out?
options: Her position on the airport surface
Her altitude above the field
The words "student pilot," since air calls skip them
Her assigned squawk code and ADS-B status
quiz.why: Initial contact: facility name, full call sign, your position when on an airport surface, then the request [[33:228|AIM 4-2-3]]. Student pilots should identify themselves on every initial contact, in the air too [[33:231|AIM 4-2-4]].

quiz.q: With a dead receiver, at about what distance does the AIM say to report your position and join the pattern at a towered airport?
options: 10 miles
1 mile
15 to 20 miles
3 to 5 miles
quiz.why: At about 3 to 5 miles, advise the tower of your position and join the pattern [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

quiz.q: At about what speed of a departing aircraft do the RELs ahead of it illuminate?
options: About 10 knots
At liftoff
About 30 knots
About 80 knots
quiz.why: When a departing aircraft reaches about 30 knots, REL arrays ahead illuminate [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].

final_quiz.q: A new learner flies well but freezes on the radio and says she will sound stupid. Which plan best fits the AIH?
options: Do all the radio work yourself until the checkride, so she can focus on flying the airplane
Tell her the radio is easy, everyone feels that way, and move on to landings
Put her straight into a busy Class C on the next flight to toughen her up quickly
Teach the shape of each call on the ground, then build from ATIS to ground to tower
final_quiz.why: Threat narrows perception and an overwhelming situation is a threat [[25:59|AIH 3-8]]; schemas let pilots catch the key items of a call [[25:62|AIH 3-11]]; build on a solid base [[25:91|AIH 3-40]].

final_quiz.q: On short final, tower gives your learner a traffic advisory while you are mid-sentence about the flare. What is best?
options: Turn the radio volume down so you can finish the point about the flare
Finish your point quickly over the tower call
Stop talking, let her hear and answer tower, and keep prompts short
Answer tower yourself while she keeps flying
final_quiz.why: Excessive coaching on final can cause missed transmissions; use concise prompting [[25:193|AIH 10-9]]. Pilots must stay vigilant on the frequency, especially on final [[33:227|AIM 4-2-1]].

final_quiz.q: At an airport with parallel runways, tower clears your learner to land on 27 Left. What should her first readback include?
options: Only her call sign, since landing clearances need no readback
"Roger" and her call sign
The runway assignment including "left", with her call sign
The wind and altimeter
final_quiz.why: The initial readback of a landing clearance should include the runway, including left, right or center [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]], and the call sign [[33:278|AIM 4-4-7]].

final_quiz.q: Approach says, "Cessna Two Kilo Lima, change to my frequency one two five point six." What is the best check-in on the new frequency?
options: A full initial call: facility name, full call sign, altitude and request
"One two five point six, Two Kilo Lima"
Nothing; listen until the controller calls
Press IDENT and wait
final_quiz.why: "Change to my frequency" means the same controller on a new frequency, so the initial callup may be abbreviated [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

final_quiz.q: Smoke fills the cabin at 600 feet after takeoff, and your learner's first move is to key the mike and explain the problem to the tower in detail. What does the RMH say about radio work in an emergency?
options: Always call ATC first, since no emergency action may start before a clearance
Make a full report to the tower before touching any checklist item
Switch to 121.5 MHz first, because only that frequency can authorize a landing
There may be no time to contact ATC, so prioritize tasks: fly and run the emergency first
final_quiz.why: There may be no time to contact ATC in an emergency; during an emergency a pilot needs to prioritize tasks and manage workload [[30:56|RMH 8-3]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner declares an emergency with approach, then wants to switch to a nearby field's CTAF to talk with traffic there. What does the AIM say?
options: Switch right away; the CTAF is always the better frequency in an emergency
Stay unless a change is absolutely necessary, and if so, tell the station first
Squawk 7600 and switch, since ATC can't help once an emergency is declared
Switch to 121.5 MHz at once, since approach can no longer work the emergency
final_quiz.why: After declaring, follow ATC's advice and do not change frequency or ground station unless absolutely necessary; if you do, advise the station first [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

final_quiz.q: Smoke appears and the learner wants to follow a checklist line that turns off the master switch. What does the AFH warn about?
options: Nothing; the master only powers the cabin lights, so the radios and the transponder stay on
Unless the fire is electrical or a crash is imminent, it kills the radios and transponder
It will stop the engine, since the magnetos run from the master switch
It turns on the ELT automatically and sends a distress signal to ATC
final_quiz.why: Deactivating the electrical system prevents using the radios for distress messages and makes ATC lose the transponder return [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner has crossed the hold line and is entering the runway with a clearance when the RELs ahead turn red. Stopping would leave her on the runway. What does the AIM say?
options: Back-taxi to the hold line at once, even though she is on the runway
Use her best judgment, knowing the runway is unsafe, and call ATC as soon as possible
Ignore the lights, because her clearance from the tower overrides them
Stop exactly where she is on the runway and wait for the lights to go out
final_quiz.why: If remaining clear is impractical for safety, for example the aircraft is already on the runway, proceed by best judgment understanding the lights mean unsafe, and contact ATC at the earliest opportunity [[33:127|AIM 2-1-6]].

final_quiz.q: Both radios are dead and your learner's planned destination is a busy Class C primary airport. A quiet non-towered airport is nearby. What do the sources suggest?
options: Circle until the radio works
Land on a highway
Continue to the Class C, since the tower's light signals will handle any arrival
Land at the quieter non-towered airport if practical, watching extra carefully
final_quiz.why: No-radio arrivals are not accepted at busy airports [[1:357|PHAK 14-23]]; a non-towered airport with less traffic may be prudent, with extra vigilance [[1:358|PHAK 14-24]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner asks whether declaring an emergency means she must file a written report. What is correct?
options: Never; declaring an emergency never brings paperwork of any kind, even if ATC asks
Yes, always, to the NTSB within 10 days of any emergency declared
Only if the FAA asks about a 91.3(b) deviation, or ATC asks after giving priority
Only if the airplane is damaged or anyone is hurt during the emergency
final_quiz.why: A written report of a deviation is sent on request of the Administrator [[60:435|14 CFR 91.3]]; after priority handling, a report within 48 hours to the facility manager if ATC requests it [[60:450|14 CFR 91.123]].

final_quiz.q: You want your learner to practice a lost-communication arrival at a Class D airport. Which plan is safest and legal?
options: Turn off both radios and fly the AIM procedure for real
Keep the radio working and handle ATC yourself while she flies and narrates the AIM lost-comm steps, after briefing it on the ground
Squawk 7600 for realism
Enter the Class D without calling to test the tower
final_quiz.why: Class D requires two-way radio communication [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129]]. Scenario training adds a radio outage with planning first [[25:183|AIH 9-13]]; the steps come from [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]. Keeping the real radio on is application.

final_quiz.q: Tower asks your learner, "Can you accept Runway 29?" The crosswind there is beyond her limit. Which reply is best?
options: "Unable Runway 29, request Runway 33," with her call sign
Say nothing and land on 33
"Wilco," then quietly land on 33 since it has less crosswind
"Roger"
final_quiz.why: Unable means you can't comply [[34:436|AIM P/C Glossary]]; accepting or refusing a clearance is the pilot's responsibility [[33:279|AIM 4-4-7]].

final_quiz.q: A transfer learner's pilot certificate carries an 'English Proficient' endorsement. What does AC 60-28B say that endorsement means?
options: That the holder passed an FAA written test in English with at least 90 percent
At least the equivalent of ICAO Operational Level 4 English proficiency
That English is the holder's first language and no check is ever needed again
That the holder may fly only inside the United States, in English-only airspace
final_quiz.why: An 'English Proficient' endorsement on a pilot certificate means the holder meets at least the equivalent of ICAO Operational Level 4 English language proficiency [[10:5|AC 60-28B 6.4]]; instructors and evaluators still check it during training and reviews [[10:4|AC 60-28B 6]].

takeaways: Fear narrows perception: lower the threat with scripts, small steps and early successes, and tell new learners to say "student pilot".
Teach the shape of each call before the words, and never coach over ATC; do the teaching before you call tower.
Read back altitudes, vectors and runways in order with the call sign; ask at once when unsure, and say unable when you can't comply.
Light gun: ground or air first, then green means yes, red means no, white means go back; only steady green clears takeoff or landing.
Before calling a radio dead, check volume, frequency, stuck mike, audio panel and the electrical system; then squawk 7600 and fly the AIM 4-2-13 procedure.
RWSL red means stop and talk to ATC; lights going dark is never a clearance.
Urgency begins at doubt: teach learners to ask for help early and that declaring an emergency is the right call.
cfi_notes: PHAK 14-23 says to acknowledge at night by blinking the landing light [[1:357|PHAK 14-23]]; the AIM says landing or navigation lights [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]. Teach the AIM.

PHAK Figure 14-43 defines SQUAWK (number) as operating in Mode A/3 [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]], while the AIM phraseology says operate on the code with altitude reporting enabled [[33:224|AIM 4-1-20]]. Teach the AIM.

AIM 6-2-2 says a pilot who wants to alert a radar facility in a distress or urgency condition should squawk 7700 [[34:29|AIM 6-2-2]]. AIM 6-3-2 adds that a pilot already in radio contact keeps the assigned code unless told otherwise, and squawks 7700 if ATC can't be reached at once [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]]. Teach the two together so learners don't change codes in the middle of an emergency ATC is already handling.

The PHAK figure and AIM TBL 4-3-1 add a column for vehicles and personnel [[1:359|PHAK 14-25]] [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]]; 14 CFR 91.125 gives only the aircraft meanings [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Test learners on the aircraft columns.
The sources are silent on teaching with ATC recordings or live streams. Treat it as technique, and make sure the learner also hears your local facilities in the airplane.
Don't simulate a radio failure by actually going silent in Class D; 14 CFR 91.129 requires two-way radio there [[60:453|14 CFR 91.129]]. Keep the real link and have the learner narrate.
On the CFI test, S3 says "or as directed by the evaluator": expect the examiner to play ATC. Read back and comply exactly as you would on the air.

The AIM says pilots should use the phonetic alphabet when identifying the aircraft on initial contact [[33:232|AIM 4-2-7]]. Drill it on the ground before the first flight so it is not one more thing to think about in the air.

AIM 4-3-13 says the only extra message a light can send is the "general warning signal" [[33:257|AIM 4-3-13]], and the light gun table lists alternating red and green as "exercise extreme caution" [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]]. Neither source says these are the same signal, so teach each as written.
gaps: The sources do not list which airports have Runway Status Lights; check the airport's current information before a trip.
No source gives a radio training syllabus, a number of practice calls before solo, or a way to measure radio readiness beyond consistent performance [[25:163|AIH 8-5]].
How a specific radio, audio panel or intercom works (squelch test, VOX, mike selector) is only in its POH/AFM supplement or avionics guide.
Battery endurance for your airplane is not in these sources; the AFH numbers are an example only [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Use the POH.
The sources don't say how a learner can see real light gun signals before needing them; ask your local tower whether a demonstration is possible.

activities.title: Know your radio stack
activities.intro: Drag each job to the numbered pin on the part of the radio stack that does it.

activities.intro: Tap a phrase, then the meaning that goes with it.

activities.title: The radio went quiet: troubleshoot in order
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Check the volume, recheck the frequency and make sure your microphone is not stuck in transmit
Recheck the radios or use another transmitter, and keep the next call short
Call "any radio" and ask for a call on a frequency you can use
Squawk 7600 and fly the lost-communication procedure

activities.title: Which radio failure is it?
activities.intro: Tap an action, then tap the failure the AIM gives it for.

items.t: Tell the tower your type, position, altitude and intention to land, and ask for light signals
Report position at 3 to 5 miles, then downwind or base on a full pattern
Monitor the tower frequency on the sectional for landing and traffic information
Rock the wings in daylight to acknowledge what the tower says on the radio
Keep visual contact with the tower and rely only on light signals

activities.title: Numbers you will brief
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: After an alternator failure, your learner turns off the pitot heat, both landing lights and the heater blower. Using AFH Figure 18-9, how many amps does that shed?
items.why: Figure 18-9: pitot heating 3.30 A, landing lights 17.80 A, heater blower motor 14.00 A [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. 3.30 + 17.80 + 14.00 = 35.1 A.

items.q: AFH Figure 18-9 lists 1 to 2 amps for each com receiver and each nav receiver, and 5 to 7 amps for a keyed transceiver. Using the high end of each range, how many amps does your learner draw while transmitting with one com receiver, one nav receiver and the transceiver keyed?
items.why: Figure 18-9: com and nav receivers 1 to 2 A each, keyed transceiver 5 to 7 A [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. 2 + 2 + 7 = 11 A while transmitting, against 2 + 2 = 4 A while only listening. Application: on a failing battery, keep calls short and few.

items.q: Your learner wants to tell flight service her ETA of 1615 Eastern Daylight Time in UTC. What four-digit time does she say?
items.why: Eastern Standard Time adds 5 hours; for daylight time subtract 1 hour [[33:234|AIM 4-2-12]]: 1615 + 5 - 1 = 1615 + 4 = 2015 UTC.

activities.title: True or false: radio procedures, failures and emergencies
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: If two-way contact fails on a new frequency during a distress or urgency, the AIM says to return at once to the frequency where you last had two-way contact.
cards.why: True. Advise the station before any change, and if two-way contact can't be made on the new frequency, return immediately [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].

cards.s: Whether a two-way radio failure is an emergency is the pilot's decision.
cards.why: True. It depends on the circumstances and is a determination made by the pilot [[34:53|AIM 6-4-1]].

cards.s: Squawking 7600 guarantees ATC will see your airplane.
cards.why: False. The aircraft may not be in radar coverage [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]].

cards.s: If ATC tells you to change frequency at a specific fix, switch right away anyway.
cards.why: False. Monitor the frequency you are on until reaching the time, fix or altitude given, unless ATC says otherwise [[33:229|AIM 4-2-3]].

cards.s: If you are in doubt which frequency to use en route, 122.2 MHz reaches most FSSs.
cards.why: True. 122.2 MHz is assigned to most FSSs as a common en route simplex frequency [[33:235|AIM 4-2-14]].

cards.s: After a radio failure, the AIM says to try the last assigned frequency first and use 121.5 MHz only if that fails.
cards.why: False. There is no priority among the last assigned frequency, an FSS or New York or San Francisco Radio, and 121.5 MHz; if you can, do all at the same time [[34:54|AIM 6-4-3]] [[34:55|AIM 6-4-3]].

activities.title: Dual cross-country: the radio fades out
activities.intro: You are the CFI on a dual VFR cross-country with flight following in a single-alternator trainer. Your learner is flying and working the radio.

steps.s: Approach, normally busy, has been silent for several minutes. Your learner reaches for the transponder to squawk 7600. What do you coach?
options: Squawk 7600 now
Check volume, frequency and a stuck mike first
Turn back home at once
Switch to 121.5 and wait
steps.why: Be alert to the lack of sounds: check volume, recheck the frequency and make sure the mike isn't stuck [[33:227|AIM 4-2-2]].

steps.s: Volume and frequency are fine, but the ammeter shows a discharge and the low-voltage light is on. Next?
options: Keep going and watch it
Shed nonessential loads, tell ATC now and ask for vectors to the nearest suitable airport
Turn off the master to save the battery for landing
Cycle the radios to test them
steps.why: Shed non-essential loads, notify ATC immediately and request vectors to the nearest suitable airport [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

steps.s: ATC vectors you toward a Class D airport 12 miles away. Then the radios die completely. Weather is good VFR. What now?
options: Enter the Class D straight away and land
Squawk 7600, stay outside or above the surface area until you know the traffic flow, then join the pattern and watch the tower
Squawk 7700 and orbit until the radio returns
Land in the nearest field
steps.why: Squawk 7600 [[34:54|AIM 6-4-2]]; with both radios dead, remain outside or above until the flow is known, join the pattern and keep visual contact with the tower [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]].

steps.s: On downwind, in daylight, the tower shows your learner a flashing green. How does she acknowledge, and what does she do next?
options: Blink the landing light and land on this pass
Rock the wings, continue the pattern and land only after a steady green
Rock the wings and land now
Do nothing until she gets a steady red
steps.why: With both radios dead, acknowledge light signals as for a dead transmitter: rock the wings in daylight [[33:235|AIM 4-2-13]]. Flashing green in flight means return for landing, to be followed by steady green at the proper time [[60:451|14 CFR 91.125]].

steps.s: Safe on the ramp, your learner asks why losing the radios raised the risk so much on a clear VFR day. What do you teach?
options: It didn't; the radio only matters in IMC
Voice radio is a hazard detector: ATC and FSS give real-time weather, traffic and airspace information
It only mattered because the transponder failed with it
Radios matter only at towered airports, never in the pattern elsewhere
steps.why: Voice radio is an effective way to find out about hazards: controllers and flight service specialists provide real-time information on weather, air traffic, airspace activity and other hazards [[30:22|RMH 3-4]].
